content.intro: In this lesson, you will study secure randomness and tokens with a short explanation, an original visual map, a Java example, and a check you can perform yourself. Focus on the relationship between the rule and the behavior rather than memorizing isolated syntax.
content.why_it_matters: This concept matters because it helps you enforce security policy at trust boundaries and use vetted platform primitives. In this lesson, focus on securerandom and use a minimal example to check what the rule actually guarantees.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Security depends on trust boundaries and explicit policy, not on a value’s Java type. Validate untrusted inputs, use standard cryptography and secure defaults, and keep secrets out of logs and source control. Apply that reasoning specifically to securerandom and confirm the result with the example or a targeted test. The important habit is to make the assumptions explicit and use the code example as a small experiment.

items.title: Distinguishing security-sensitive randomness from ordinary random numbers
items.text: Network calls can fail or stall even when request code is correct. Use the standard HTTP client, validate destinations and responses, configure timeouts, and apply bounded retries only where safe.

items.title: Protecting generated secrets
items.text: Use vetted platform cryptography and secure defaults rather than inventing protocols. Validate at trust boundaries, keep secrets out of source and logs, and separate authentication from authorization.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating input or configuration as trusted just because it is typed as a Java String.
common_mistakes.why: Types describe representation; they do not prove that input meets the application policy.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate at trust boundaries, keep secrets out of logs, and reject invalid input explicitly.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing only a single happy path.
common_mistakes.why: Boundary values and failures often reveal assumptions hidden by the simplest example.
common_mistakes.fix: Add an empty, boundary, or invalid case and state the expected behavior before running it.

common_mistakes.why: It becomes difficult to identify the actual cause of a different result.
common_mistakes.fix: Change one factor at a time and keep a short record of observed behavior.
